paragraph.text: C13. "I honor the animals I eat"

gratitude is a sincere feeling in the person who eats, but it changes nothing for the animal: they lose their life all the same. Honoring someone usually means respecting their interests, and an animal's greatest interest is to go on living without suffering. When eating animals isn't necessary to survive, the clearest way to honor them is not to make them suffer or die. Many Indigenous traditions thank the hunted animal in subsistence settings, and that deserves respect; but meat bought at the supermarket comes from anonymous animals, bred and slaughtered on an industrial scale.
"I don't eat on autopilot. I thank the animal before every meal and waste nothing. I honor the animals I eat."
We are part of nature, and every living thing feeds on others.
The moral problem lies in waste, indifference and cruelty, not in the act of eating.
Someone who eats with gratitude, without waste, recognizes the animal's value.
So eating animals with that attitude is morally acceptable.

P1 is true, but doesn't say what we should do (see C7). P2 is the decisive premise and is false: for the animal, the main problem is being killed. P3 describes the attitude of the one who eats, not what happens to the one who is eaten.
"I thank the animal before I eat."
"The animal offers itself, and I honor that sacrifice."
"I eat the whole animal, nose to tail, out of respect."
"An ethics of care is expressed in a respectful relationship with food."
"We are animals and part of the ecosystem; no one lives without impact." (which is C7)

Saying thank you is lovely. But if someone took your favorite toy and then said "thank you very much", the toy would still be gone. For the animal, a thank-you doesn't give their life back. The best way to show you care about them is to let them live.

The gratitude is sincere, but it changes nothing for the animal: they lose their life all the same. Honoring someone usually means respecting what matters to them, and what matters most to an animal is staying alive and not suffering. When we don't need to eat animals to live, the clearest way to honor them is not to make them suffer or die.
"If the animal could choose, would they prefer to be thanked or to stay alive?"
The attitude of the one who eats
Awareness of where food comes from

text.bold: 1. Gratitude lives in the one who eats, not in the one who is eaten.

paragraph.text: The feeling can be real and deep, but it doesn't reach the animal. They were bred, transported and slaughtered the same way.

When we say we honor a person, we mean we take seriously what matters to them. Killing them and then thanking them wouldn't be honoring them. The same holds for an animal who has an interest in living.

text.bold: 3. Not wasting is good, but doesn't solve the main thing.

paragraph.text: Using the whole animal reduces waste, but doesn't reduce the number of animals killed.

In many Indigenous traditions, thanking the hunted animal is part of a subsistence relationship without easy alternatives, and those traditions deserve respect (see D7). Someone who buys meat at the supermarket, with alternatives available, is in a very different situation: the animal came from an industrial, anonymous supply chain.
Being part of the ecosystem doesn't settle how much harm to cause
Subsistence traditions are a different case from urban consumption
(d) The strongest counter-reply: indifference is the real evil
The most serious version says the problem with modern animal farming is turning animals into things, and that eating mindfully and with gratitude restores a lost relationship of respect.

It's true that indifference toward animals is a problem, that wasting is worse than using, that thinking about where food comes from is better than eating on autopilot, and that subsistence traditions that thank the animal deserve respect.
But the gratitude of the one who eats changes nothing for the one who is eaten. When we don't need to eat animals to live, the clearest way to honor them is not to make them suffer or die.
